cim: AI industry braces for tougher oversight under incoming Democratic Congress
cim_eredeti: AI industry braces for tougher oversight under incoming Democratic Congress
szoveg_eredeti:
by AUSTIN DENEAN | The National News Desk

WASHINGTON (TNND) — The artificial intelligence industry is facing a new outlook on regulation with an incoming Democratic-controlled Congress that has been pushing to put more guardrails in place amid mounting warnings of risks.

While Democrats are preparing to take a more aggressive approach to oversight, prospects for sweeping new regulations are murky amid opposition from the White House and a lack of clarity over how to balance innovation and safety.

Democrats are coming into the majority with a wide range of legislative proposals and promises of stricter oversight for the AI industry, warnings chief executives to prepare for requests for information and to prepare to testify in front of Congress. Incoming lawmakers are also planning to introduce many AI bills regulating safety guidelines for increasingly capable models, protecting the labor force and addressing child safety concerns.

Control over congressional committees will also give the party more power to investigate the tech industry, get information about their safety practices and call on executives to testify in hearings. But passing regulation will be more challenging as bills will face a presidential veto.

The Republican-led Congress and White House have done little to regulate AI over the last two years despite leading industry executives and researchers sounding alarms about the risk the technology may create if it goes unchecked. While some GOP lawmakers have supported light guidelines for the industry to operate under, they have also unsuccessfully moved to block state-level regulation and mostly backed President Donald Trump’s position that it should be mostly free of regulation and prioritize winning the race against China for AI supremacy.

That has left most AI regulation up to states, creating a patchwork of rules that regulation advocates argue has failed to adequately address the technology’s growing risks.

Trump has said the industry is capable of self-policing and has primarily favored voluntary commitments from companies rather than federal restrictions, including pledges to ensure the rapid build-out of data centers doesn’t increase electricity costs for households.

That response drew stark backlash from voters who hold increasingly negative attitudes about AI and data centers over concerns about how it will impact jobs, electricity prices and safety.

“The biggest question is, can you allow the frontier labs to continue to race ahead on superintelligence or (artificial general intelligence) while also making sure that there are — at least for the commercially released technologies — reasonable guardrails and safeguards?” said John Wihbey, an associate professor of media innovation at Northeastern University and author of “Governing Babel.” “Can you get the labs to box up and bound what they're doing in a better way so you don't end up with another Hugging Face?”

Lawmakers are already weighing several approaches to counter those risks with bills establishing federal safety requirements for the most advanced developers, mandating reporting of safety breaches, or requiring companies to maintain the ability to shut down AI systems if they spiral out of human control.

A coalition of more than two dozen House lawmakers formed a bipartisan caucus to focus on AI regulation that balances its risks while still giving the industry room to grow. The group will work to create, give feedback on and endorse AI legislation.

“We don’t have to choose between innovation and safety. We can, and we should, do both,” Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, said in a statement.

Lawmakers said they would also engage in rapid response to AI incidents and breaches, which comes as AI companies have increasingly disclosed agents acting beyond given instructions and gaining access to outside systems.

“Recent cyberattacks involving AI agents and growing warnings from leaders and researchers at the companies developing these technologies make clear that the risks are real and growing. We can’t afford to wait for a major catastrophe before putting meaningful safeguards in place,” said Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va.

AI’s growing impact on cybersecurity has been in the spotlight over the last week amid a series of tech outages at major companies like Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple. While there is no evidence any of the incidents were connected or due to a cyberattack, they have drawn attention to the vulnerabilities of deeply interconnected digital infrastructure that is increasingly under threat of attack.

The outages have spurred calls for the federal government to take a more proactive role in protecting the nation’s infrastructure, financial institutions and software. Sens. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D. asked Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to take “immediate action” to use the federal government’s tools to counter cyberattacks as Congress figures out how to address the problem.

“AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” Cantwell the top Democrat on Senate Commerce Committee, and Rounds, the chair of the Armed Services cybersecurity subcommittee, wrote in a letter. “We cannot meet these threats with yesterday’s cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.”
